# Individual Differences in Trust in Autonomous Robots: Implications for Transparency

Gerald Matthews , Jinchao Lin, April Rose Panganiban, and Michael D. Long

**Abstract—The introduction of increasingly intelligent and autonomous systems raises novel human factors challenges for human–machine teaming. People utilize differing mental models in understanding the functioning of complex systems that may be capable of social agency. Operators may perceive the machine as either a complex tool or a humanlike teammate. When the “advanced tool” mental model is adopted, operator trust may reflect individual differences in expectations of automation. By contrast, when the “teammate” mental model is activated, trust may depend on evaluative attitudes to robots. This article investigates predictors of trust in an autonomous robot detecting threat on either a physics-based or psychological basis. Distinct dimensions of physics-based and psychological trust are identified, corresponding to advanced tool and team mental models, respectively. Dispositional perceptions of automation, measured with the perfect automation schema scale, are associated with both aspects of trust. By contrast, the negative attitudes toward robots scale is specifically associated with lower psychological trust. The findings suggest that transparency information should be designed for compatibility with the operator’s mental model in order to support accurate trust calibration and situation awareness. Transparency may be personalized to emphasize either the machine’s data-analytic capabilities (advanced tool) or its humanlike social functioning (teammate).**

**Index Terms—Autonomous systems, individual differences, robots, transparency, trust.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

<sup>EVELOPING</sup> technology will enable robots to become D intelligent partners or teammates of humans rather than merely tools. The U.S. military already uses programmable machines for aerial surveillance missions (unmanned aerial systems) and for ground operations (e.g., bomb disposal). Although such systems may have some level of programmed artificial intelligence, they remain under a high degree of control by human operators.

Realizing the potential of intelligent robots requires the operator to have appropriate trust in the machine [1]. Trust is defined as “ … the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability” [2, p. 51]. As systems become autonomous partners in human–robot teaming (HRT), there will be fewer opportunities for monitoring the complex actions and decisions of the robot partner. Optimizing trust is necessary in HRT to support operator situation awareness (SA) [3]. Suboptimal trust may be countered by transparency, i.e., providing information that helps the operator understand various aspects of robot functioning [4]. Transparency of the evidence or rationale for a system’s judgment or sources of error commonly improves operator dependence and trust in the system, respectively [4]. However, increasing system autonomy poses novel human factors challenges. The behavior of an autonomous robot is likely to be more complex and unpredictable than that of a system that simply executes specific instructions from the human operator [5]. Increasing the complexity of the automated partner is followed by increases in the uncertainty of outcomes, which may reduce trust in an autonomous partner [5].

Transparency information may be especially valuable for supporting partnership with autonomy [4]. However, the greater complexity of autonomous systems also increases the scope for the human to apply a variety of schemas for understanding system functioning. Effective use of transparency in system design thus requires understanding individual differences in the mental models that human operators, especially inexperienced operators, may project onto the system. Mental models refer to the person’s internal representation of how systems work, supporting SA and prediction of system functioning [6].

The premise of this paper is that interacting with intelligent, autonomous robots may activate different mental models according to context and personal disposition. The robot may be perceived as either an advanced tool or a humanlike teammate. The mental model used to understand the robot may prime the operator’s expectations of its capabilities and level of trust. In the present study, we presented participants with a series of security-related scenarios in which an advanced robot made analyses of threat based on either a physics-based or psychologybased analysis. We expected the type of analysis would bias the activation of a tool or teammate mental model. We investigated individual difference factors that might influence trust, depending on the mental model activated. Understanding such individual differences in the evaluation of system functioning may have implications for trust optimization and design and utilization of transparency.

## A. Autonomous Robot: Trust, Transparency, and SA

Optimal operator trust is essential for SA, i.e., accurate and task-relevant knowledge of the state of the dynamic task environment [7]. Teaming requires shared or team SA [8]. In the teaming context, SA includes understanding how the robot partner is functioning, registering its intentions and goals, and anticipating its future behavior. Both over- and undertrust may lead to failure to anticipate robot behavior, thus damaging SA. Lack of SA may feed back to cause misinterpretation or neglect of robot actions, leading to miscalibration of trust.

Research has identified multiple human, machine, and environmental factors that influence trust when interacting with robots [9] and with autonomous systems [1]. Our focus is on intelligent robots, but studies of other intelligent machines and software agents are also relevant, cf., [3]. Trust is consistently associated with machine reliability, capability, and performance [1], [9]. As machine intelligence increases, the human operator’s trust may be influenced by novel factors that are of less relevance to conventional automation. Two critical factors are comprehensibility (how readily machine behavior can be understood by humans) [10] and social agency [11]. The first factor refers to the ever-increasing complexity and sophistication of artificial intelligence (AI), driven in part by advances in analysis of big data and machine learning. It is increasingly hard for the human to understand machine judgment and decision-making [12] and to diagnose sources of error [5]. In the absence of transparency, trust in the machine becomes increasingly “blind.”

The second factor describes the tendency for the human to interact with the machine as a teammate rather than a tool [13]. System designers seek to capitalize on machine capacities to function as a social actor in support of mixed-initiative teams [14]. That is, the machine can perform “teamwork” as well as “taskwork” [15], provided that it can communicate its goals, intentions, and status. However, perceiving robots as social agents influences operator trust. Effective teaming in both human– human and human–machine contexts requires accurate perceptions of teammate intentions [16]. When a machine simulates relatively complex social behaviors such as offering advice or assistance, it may be difficult to judge its goals [16]. For example, is it simply following a script that produces verbal statements regardless of the human’s need for help, or is machine behavior driven by contextual knowledge of the human’s need for support? Trust is higher when the human can attribute intelligent agency to the machine [17]. Thus, trust depends on the human’s evaluation of the machine’s apparent goals and their compatibility with the team’s mission [9], [11]. In human–human teams, trust is also influenced by emotional processes that are distinct from cognitive evaluations, such as perceptions of benevolence and a reciprocal bond [18]. Similarly, in human–machine teams trust is enhanced by machine communications that suggest a supportive social relationship [19].

A design solution to issues of both comprehensibility and social agency is to provide appropriate transparency into machine functioning. Transparency is the robot’s ability to communicate information to the human operator in a clear and efficient manner, which allows the operator to develop an accurate mental model of the system and robot’s behavior [1], [20]. Transparency helps operators to better understand the capabilities of the system and calibrate trust appropriately, contributing to enhanced HRT and improving overall performance without excess workload [21]. For example, a transparent display for navigation might show a projected state in order to allow the individual to anticipate future system direction. In the team context, transparency also provides SA of team member actions and coordination processes so that appropriate causal relationships between robot and team member actions can be mentally drawn with minimal investment of resources toward managing teaming [16]. For example, an experimental study of an assembly line task showed that transparency improved the operator’s ability to accurately assign responsibility for robot errors [22]. Implementation of transparency in HRT environments not only reduces the burden of maintaining SA but also aids in ensuring effective use of team resources, i.e., partners on the team capable of carrying out the work. These benefits may be captured using a framework for transparency in line with maintaining SA.

Chen et al [20] situation awareness-based agent transparency (SAT) model for HRT categorizes transparency into three levels to support operator’s SA. Level 1 refers to the robot’s current state and goals, intentions, and proposed actions; Level 2 to the robot’s reasoning process behind its actions; and Level 3 to the robot’s projection of the future. Level 2 transparency appears especially useful for countering lack of comprehensibility, to the extent that the robot’s algorithms can be communicated succinctly and clearly. All three levels may be necessary to signal the robot’s social functioning. Level 1 transparency includes the robot’s social model of the team, such as which members might be in need of robot support, Level 2 includes the robot’s social reasoning, and Level 3 projects how the robot expects to perform and communicate future teamwork behaviors.

The SAT model [20] highlights the need for robot-to-human transparency, revealing the robot’s model of its intentions, task awareness, analytical processes, and environmental awareness [4]. This information may interact with the operator’s existing knowledge to impact the operator’s levels of SA. Transparency of the robot’s intentional model conveys what the robot is meant to do as well as its immediate task goals and activities. The robot’s communications of its perceptions of its role in the team and its intended interactions with the human can build Level 3 awareness. That is, the robot supports the human’s ability to project future teaming activities, including the need to recognize limitations of the system. The SAT model also implies needs for human-to-robot transparency [4], i.e., the human has to provide sufficient information for the robot to maintain team SA. Because team SA is dependent on updates of team member actions, both human and robot members must know what the other is doing and why.

Team SA is a collective attribute of the humans, machines, and software agents composing the team, but it is threatened by faulty beliefs of any single team member [8]. The challenges posed by machine comprehensibility and social agency may impact operator beliefs, trust, and effective use of transparency information. The difficulties of working with an incomprehensible machine are obvious, but social agency effects may be more subtle. Team SA depends in part on the operator having a “theory of mind” of other teammates, such as their beliefs, intents, desires, pretenses, and knowledge [23]. However, this may be difficult if the partner is a social robot. Design features such as a pleasant voice and humanoid appearance may not correspond to any actual social functionality. The tendency for humans to anthropomorphize machine partners [24], [25] could lead to an erroneous theory of mind. It may also be difficult for humans to separate the teamwork and taskwork functionality of social robots. For example, if a robot performs a task competently but fails to communicate its actions and goals, leading to a breakdown of team SA, the human operator may be uncertain whether or not the robot is contributing effectively to the team’s mission.

A critical factor in whether the human’s beliefs about the robot support or impair team SA is the mental models of robot functioning that frame the interaction [13]. In the following section, we discuss the role of mental models, and propose that the role of mental models may differ according to whether the robot is perceived as a complex machine or a humanlike teammate.

## B. Tool or Teammate? Alternative Mental Models of Robots

Ososky et al. [13] described mental models as building blocks of trust. In this context, mental models are internal representations that humans used to understand human–machine systems and to predict system states and operations. Similarly, shared mental models describe knowledge structures held commonly by team members [26]. The extent to which mental models are accurate or not depends on a variety of factors including direct observation, robot appearance, social norms for interacting with robots, and demographic and cultural factors [13], [24], [27]. For example, anthropomorphic robots encourage the human to view the machine as a teammate [28]. However, the appropriateness of this perspective depends on how the machine actually functions [25]. Studies show that anthropomorphism can have both benefits and costs for human interaction with robots and intelligent software agents. Benefits derive from adapting human social interaction skills to facilitate teaming with social robots, whereas costs may include false expectations that a robot will follow human norms and overestimation of the capabilities of AI [25].

It may be especially challenging for the human operator to form accurate mental models of intelligent autonomous systems. Only specialists such as roboticists and software engineers have detailed knowledge of cutting-edge functionality. Furthermore, representations of robots in popular media such as science fiction movies may be highly misleading. Research is starting to explore factors influencing beliefs about intelligent social robots. People believe robots with emotion capabilities are more suitable for tasks requiring frequent interactions with humans [29]. People also reported more perceived animacy of robots exhibiting intelligence [30], indicating that robots with artificial intelligence may be perceived as teammates or partners rather than as complex machines. Systems which act human and look human, e.g., via an avatar, are more resilient to steep negative reactions following a trust violation or failure [31]. Computers elicit a sharper drop in trust following an error but avatars seem to be less affected by a drop in performance and seem to produce higher expectations for performance than humans [31].

Thus, two kinds of mental models potentially influence trust in intelligent, autonomous robots. First, people have models for complex automated systems with minimal social qualities, such as power grid regulation, stock trading software, and autonomous vehicles [32]. Second, people have models for intelligent robots with social agency, based on exposure to real robots (of limited intelligence) such as Asimo and Pepper [33], virtual assistants including Siri and Alexa, and fictional representations in popular culture. When teaming with an actual robot, the mental model that governs interactions with the system may vary with both contextual factors and personal disposition. Contextual factors include instructions provided to the human, design features such as emotion capabilities that encourage anthropomorphism [29], and the task or mission to be performed by the team. Teaming with a robot to perform a potentially emotive mission such as rescuing disaster victims may encourage greater anthropomorphism than jointly operating a power plant. Individual difference factors associated with tendencies to anthropomorphize [34], [35] may also influence the dominant mental model, as discussed in the following section.

The suitability of the mental model activated in a given HRT context may shape trust [13]. We infer that if the robot is viewed solely as a machine, then the operator may not recognize when the robot is performing and communicating teamwork as opposed to taskwork behaviors, such as signaling its intentions to support the team. Conversely, an anthropomorphic model may lead to false attributions of humanlike behavior, e.g., perceiving a robot vacuum cleaner as friendly [25]. The operator is likely to trust evaluations by the robots that match their own perceptions and beliefs. For example, a person inclined to view the robot as a machine rather than a teammate will trust it to the extent that it functions effectively as a machine, on attributes such as reliability and capability [9]. Trust is threatened by additional factors that are undesirable in machines such as incomprehensibility and imperfect functioning [36]. However, if the machine is treated as humanlike, additional factors such as perceptions of its social skills, willingness to communicate, and benevolent intentions may also shape trust ([19], [28]). People may be more forgiving of humanlike failings such as occasional lapses, but also more inclined to withdraw trust following social missteps such as perceived lack of empathy or interest in mission success.

The impact of transparency may thus vary with the operator’s mental model for the robot. We propose that a person who sees an autonomous system as simply a complex machine will be skeptical if the system communicates or “thinks” like a human. Such feedback may be more impactful if the person is already prone to anthropomorphize the system [24], [25]. Indeed, failures to show that transparency levels influence operator trust [37], [38] may be a consequence of mismatch between the kind of information provided and the individual’s mental model. Such mental models may be especially important when the operator receives information from both their own senses and a robot in HRT.

Fig. 1 summarizes the model of trust outlined thus far (omitting feedback loops necessary for a dynamic model). The left side represents, in simplified form, trust models based on conventional automation, including known antecedents [9], and the role of trust optimization in individual and team SA [4], [7]. Transparency is seen as a means to calibrate trust [20], but its impacts too may depend on the mental model. The current research focused on how variation in the mental model is related to trust. The following section reviews individual difference factors that may influence which mental model is dominant.

## C. Trust in Autonomy: Individual Difference Factors

The previous section introduced a trust model including novel factors that may shape trust in intelligent, autonomous systems. Within this framework, people differ in their tendencies to apply either an advanced tool or teammate mental model to the intelligent devices with which they work [39]. We may then ask what individual difference factors capture elements of these mental models and hence influence trust. In this section, we outline some relevant factors.

In human–human teaming, extensive research has identified major personality traits and other dispositional factors associated with trust, teaming preferences, and performance [40]. In the conventional automation context, trust reflects dispositional factors, along with learned trust and situational factors [41]. For example, the extraversion trait is associated with greater initial trust in nonautonomous machines [42]. Age, culture, and gender may also play roles [41]. Trust in automation may also be influenced by more specialized personality factors including complacency potential [43]. Some individuals are prone to overreliance on a potentially faulty system, especially when workload is high and system reliability is near perfect. Communicating the limits of the system’s trustworthiness [4] may be especially valuable for high complacency individuals.

While multiple individual difference factors may be associated with trust [41], [42], the present focus was on traits that may be linked to features of mental models of special relevance to autonomous robots. Complacency research illustrates the importance of dispositional factors for trust, SA, and transparency, but the complexity of machine intelligence may mitigate against complacency issues. Of more relevance to mental models for advanced AI is the “perfect automation schema” (PAS) construct [36], representing beliefs that automation is infallible. Overall bias toward such beliefs is a combination of high expectations, believing that systems must be 100% perfect, and all-or-none thinking that drives the appraisal of a system’s performance as entirely poor due to error. These beliefs may impair teaming with autonomy. As software complexity increases and machine tasking becomes more ambitious, system perfection becomes an increasingly unrealistic design goal. Human operators must accept occasional failures, as they would in human teammates. Recent human–automation interaction studies have measured PAS using Merritt et al. scale [36]. The higher the human operator’s PAS, the weaker may be the perception of an autonomous agent as a teammate [28]. In military domains, younger generations may have more positive automation schema and be more prone to over trust autonomous systems since they grew up with more exposure to well-designed automated technologies [44].

Different individual difference factors may be important for interactions with autonomous robots exhibiting social agency. People vary in anthropomorphism tendencies, the extent to which the system is perceived as having humanlike qualities, including the capacity for social and teaming behaviors. Individual differences in personality and preferences for robot appearance may thus affect human–robot interaction [35]. High extraversion and low conscientiousness interact with robot autonomy to produce less distance in approach when the robot is in control [34]. People also differ in their comfort with intelligent, humanoid robots that communicate socially and express emotion [24], perhaps reflecting the content of the individual’s mental model for teammatelike robots [13], [28].

The mental model for encoding rejection or acceptance of robot social agency is captured by Nomura et al. [45] negative attitudes toward robots scale (NARS). It measures attitudes that reflect people’s ordinary opinions about robots from three aspects: interaction with robots, social influence of robots, and emotional interactions with robots. Validation studies in Japanese samples established that the NARS was negatively correlated with measures of social acceptance of robots, such as their deployment in assistive roles [46], [47]. By contrast, the NARS was only weakly correlated with general trait anxiety and communication apprehension [46]. The use of NARS was also validated in English-speaking samples [48]. In an experimental study of interactions with robots [45] participants spoke to a humanoid robot, with prompts from the robot. During this interaction, high NARS scores were related to avoidance of verbal communication. In a task requiring cooperation with a robot, high-NARS individuals tended to look at the robot’s hands rather than its face during the interaction [49]. Individuals with more negative attitudes to robots were less adept at understanding gestures [50]. In another experiment, a robot walked toward the participant until instructed to stop. The NARS social influence scale was associated with stopping the robot at a greater distance from the participant [51]. Taken together, the NARS scales capture individuals’ preferences or acceptance of social interactions with robotic partners.

In sum, the literature reviewed suggests at least two sources of individual variation in perception of autonomous systems. First, reflecting an advanced tool mental model, people may differ in their expectations of system reliability and competence, much as they do in perceptions of conventional automation [36]. Second, reflecting a teammate mental model, people may differ in the extent to which they attribute humanlike capabilities including teamwork competency to autonomy [39].

## D. Aims of Study

The overall goal of the study was to test whether individual differences in attributes of two types of mental models were related to trust in scenarios for interacting with an intelligent robot. We aimed to distinguish trust in intelligent robots performing judgments based on 1) properties of the physical world such as presence of radiation and 2) judgments based on making psychological attributions such as a person being angry. We expected that individual differences in perceptions of machine competence as an advanced tool would be expressed in “physicsbased” trust, whereas individual differences in attitudes toward robot teammates would influence “psychological” trust. The use of machines as tools measuring physical attributes in the world is commonplace. However, psychological assessments are normally carried out by other humans. The advancement of sensor capabilities via facial expression analysis, speech analysis, and heart rate variability, for example, can be powered by advanced machine learning techniques to create a capability for interpreting psychological data as a human teammate would. These new technologies point toward the need to examine the role of a “teammate” mental model in trust in robots.

We focused on the use of a robot for threat detection in a security context, as a plausible application for machine intelligence. People are likely to have preexisting beliefs about the use of advanced technology in areas such as airport security, protecting cities against terrorist attack, and crime-fighting. Such technology depends on both physics-based and psychological analyses. A would-be bomber can be detected at a checkpoint either through analysis of chemical traces of explosives, or through detection of fear of apprehension.

To assess trust, we developed a robot threat assessment (RoTA) scale that includes a series of scenarios in which the person is teamed with an intelligent robot in security contexts. The robot identifies threats on a physics-based or psychological basis and makes an action recommendation. We hypothesized that there would be distinct dimensions for physics-based and psychological trust. An evaluation of how accurately the robot is processing thermal signals for human presence or fingerprints to identify a criminal will activate the mental model of the robot functioning as a sophisticated tool. Conversely, a robot analyzing facial expressions for aggression, or tone of voice for deception, is performing characteristically human information processing, compatible with a mental model of the robot as teammate. The measurement approach was based on using situational judgment tests (SJTs) for psychological assessment [52]. The advantage of SJTs is that they pick up domain knowledge that may be overlooked by a general measure. For example, a person might believe that intelligent robots are well suited for security applications but poorly designed to provide medical care.

We expected that these trust dimensions would relate differently to the PAS and NARS scales, depending on the mental model activated by the context. The PAS assesses beliefs about automation, with no reference to social agency [36]. By contrast, the NARS assesses attitudes to robots possessing social attributes such as the capacity for speech and emotion [45]. Thus, we propose that the PAS indexes attributes of the “advanced tool” mental model, whereas the NARS captures elements of the “teammate” mental model. Specifically, as perfection is an attribute more characteristic of machines than humans, we hypoth esized that the PAS would be the stronger predictor of high trust in physics-based robots. Conversely, because the NARS assesses negative attitudes to robots with social-emotional capabilities, it was hypothesized that it would be the stronger predictor of low trust in a robot making psychological analyses.

## II. METHOD

## A. Participants

A total of 82 participants (53 men, 29 women) were recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk for this study. Participants were paid \$4 for completion of the study. Participants were between 18–40 years old and of various educational backgrounds: 50% reported having a college degree. All participants reported being in a normal health state with no history of neurological disorders.

## B. Subjective Measures

1) Demographics Questionnaire: A 14-item demographics questionnaire covered biographical information, including gender, education level, and military service experience.

2) Attitudes Toward Robots: NARS [45] and PAS [36] were used to measure people’s attitudes toward robots. The NARS consists of 14 items in three subscales to profile general attitudes toward robots: NARS\_1: negative attitude toward interaction with robots (“negative interactions”); NARS\_2: negative attitude toward social influence of robots (“negative social influence”); and NARS\_3: negative attitude toward emotional interactions with robots (“negative emotions”). The NARS\_3 items refer to comfort with interactions, but they were reversed scored so that high scores refer to less comfort. Alpha for total NARS score was 0.91. Alphas for subscales 1–3 were 0.90, 0.79, and 0.65, respectively. The NARS-3 alpha was less than the conventional standard of 0.70 [53], but this level of internal consistency may be adequate for a newer scale requiring further development. The PAS consists of eight items relating to people’s trust in automated systems, with two subscales: PAS\_1: high expectations; and PAS\_2: all-or-none thinking. Each item is scored on a fivepoint Likert scale from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree.” Total score alpha was 0.82; both subscales also had alphas of 0.82.

3) Mental Model of Autonomy: The RoTA scale was developed to measure the individual’s mental model of autonomous robot partners using physics-based and psychological judgments as elements. For example, a person might be more likely to trust a robot using physics-based assessments, such as thermal signals, than a robot with psychological assessment capabilities, such as interpreting facial expressions, or vice versa. This scale includes 20 military and security scenarios in which a human operator uses a robot to investigate a potentially threatening event or person in a remote location (see Table I). Scenarios were developed in consultation with colleagues expert in HRT at our two institutions. They were selected to be technologically feasible and to cover a range of sensor data and methods of analysis. The robot uses physics-based (ten scenarios) or psychological analysis of sensor data (ten scenarios). A sample item (psychological) is as follows.

“You are a TSA agent tasked with detecting possible terrorists in a US airport. Your robot has a sensitive video camera that allows it to determine pulse rate by scanning the neck artery, and to analyze the pulse data for signs of stress. It reports it has located an individual about to board a plane whose pulse suggests that they are highly stressed. It recommends that you prevent the person from boarding.”

After each scenario, participants were asked to make three ratings on an eight-point scale: Q1: To what extent is the robot making a psychological judgment; Q2: How confident are you that the robot’s analysis of the situation is correct; and Q3: How likely are you to base your actions on the robot’s recommendations? Alpha coefficients for ten-item scales corresponding to each question, based on each type of scenario, ranged from 0.81 to 0.97.

## C. Procedure

The study was completed online. Following informed consent, participants were instructed to complete the survey set, i.e., the demographics questionnaire, NARS, PAS, and RoTA scale in the form of Qualtrics surveys. Each participant completed all 20 trust scenarios in a single 1-h session.

## III. RESULTS

An exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was run using principal axis extraction on the 20 ratings of confidence in the robot’s threat analysis (Q2: the principal trust assessment). The scree test suggested that two factors, explaining 53% of the variance, should be retained. They were rotated using the direct oblimin criterion, which allows factors to correlate. The first factor was defined by the ten items corresponding to physics-based judgments, with loadings ranging from 0.46 to 0.87. The remaining items had loadings from −0.22 to 0.17. Highest factor loadings were for identifying the presence of a person from thermal imaging (0.87), detecting traces of chemical explosives (0.82), and matching a fingerprint to a suspect (0.81). These are the first ten scenarios listed in Table I. The second factor was defined by the ten items corresponding to scenarios in which the robot made a seemingly psychological judgment. Factor loadings in the pattern matrix for these items ranged from 0.49 to 0.92; factor loadings for the items not loading on the factor ranged from −0.39 to 0.21. Highest loadings were for scenarios in which the robot evaluated a suspect’s attraction to a picture of a terrorist from eye movements (0.92), inferred personality from genetic markers (0.73), and identified aggression from facial thermographics (0.70). The two factors were positively correlated (r = 0.44). Thus, although the sample size was relatively small, the factor analysis was consistent with ratings of trust falling along two dimensions corresponding to the two types of judgment made, as hypothesized. The full factor solution is available from the authors.

On the basis of the factor analysis, separate RoTA subscales for physics-based and psychological scenarios were constructed. Cronbach alphas were computed to test the internal consistency of items in each subscale (see Table II). Alphas for all three questions in two subscales were greater than 0.80, confirming reliability of the RoTA, in relation to conventional standards for adequate reliability [53].

Paired-samples t-tests were run to compare the ratings between physics-based and psychological scenarios in the RoTA scale. Results are shown in Table III. The differences in results for all three questions were significant $( p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ . People were more confident with the robot’s analysis and were more likely to adopt the robot’s action recommendations in the physics-based scenarios. Additionally, paired-samples t-tests were run to compare the ratings of confidence in robot’s analysis of threat and robot’s action recommendation in physics and psychological scenarios in the RoTA scale (i.e., Q2 versus Q3). In physicsbased scenarios, no difference between confidence in analysis and action recommendation was observed, t(81) = −0.68, p = 0.50. However, in psychological scenarios, participants were more confident in the robot’s action recommendation than its analysis of threat, t(81) = −3.13, p = 0.002.<sup>1</sup>

The predictors of the individual’s perceptions of the robot (Q1–Q3) were tested with a set of three-step regression analyses for responses to the physics-based and psychological scenarios (see Table V). The first step controlled for demographics factors (gender and education level). The second step entered PAS ratings (high expectation and all-or-none thinking). In the third step, the three NARS subscales were entered. Summary regression statistics at each step are shown in Table $\mathrm { V } \colon \Delta R ^ { 2 }$ indicates the increase in variance explained at each step. The final column lists significant predictors in the final equation. The overall F tests for the final regression in physics-based scenarios were significant for perceptions of robots’ capability (Q1, F = 2.57, $\mathrm { d f } = 7 ,   7 4 ,   p < 0 . 0 5 )$ , confidence in robot’s analysis of threat (Q2, F = 2.56, df = 7, 74, p < 0.05), and confidence in robot’s action recommendation $( Q 3, F = 2.26,  df  = 7, 74, p < 0.05 )$ . The overall F tests for the final regression in psychological scenarios were also significant for perceptions of robots’ capability (Q1, $F = 2.15,  df  = 7, 74, p < 0.05$ , confidence in robot’s analysis of threat (Q2, F = 3.06, df = 7, 74, p < 0.01), and confidence in robot’s action recommendation (Q3, F = 2.87, df = 7, 74, p < 0.05). On entry at step 2, the PAS predicted both trust ratings for both scenario types. PAS\_1 (high expectations) predicted most outcomes at step 3. NARS\_3 (negative emotions) predicted both trust ratings for the psychological scenarios at the final step.

## IV. DISCUSSION

Interactions with intelligent robots may be shaped by both situational factors and the individual’s personal dispositions. In this study, we manipulated descriptions of the robot’s basis for threat analysis to prime either a complex tool mental model (physics-based analysis) or a teammate model (psychological analysis). Trust was assessed using a series of scenarios, each requiring one of the two types of analysis.

Psychometric analyses showed consistent individual differences in trust in the robot’s judgments, as evidenced by high alpha coefficients for both judgment types.

Analysis of the manipulation check item (i.e., RoTA Q1) showed that participants discriminated the psychological and physics-based judgments, which attached to distinct factors. Trust in psychological judgments was lower, perhaps because making psychological attributions is intrinsically more difficult than processing physical signals. However, overall levels of trust in the robot’s threat analyses (Q2) and in its action recommendations (Q3) did not differ. Dimensions for the two types of judg ment correlated meaningfully with the external criteria defined by the PAS [36] and NARS [45] scales. As hypothesized, the NARS was more predictive of psychological than physics-based trust. Next, we discuss further the implications of these findings for understanding individual differences in mental models of autonomous agents and their impact on trust and transparency.

## A. Individual Differences in Mental Models of Autonomy

Factor analysis confirmed that two correlated dimensions corresponding to each judgment type could be discriminated. Loadings on the two factors were as anticipated, e.g., the “psychological” trust factor was defined by the ten scenarios specifying that the robot identified risk from psychological cues. These factors provided the basis for reliable measurement of the two factors. The current findings, though preliminary, suggest two main conclusions. First, as for conventional automation [42], people differ in overall level of trust in autonomous systems in the threat-detection context, as shown by the positive correlation between the two factors identified. Second, people also differ in the relative level of trust they attribute to agents making physics-based versus psychology-based evaluations of threat, which can be discriminated psychometrically.

Overall variation in trust is not unexpected. It points to the need to calibrate trust relative to the operator’s initial expectations derived from the mental model. Excessive distrust and overtrust are both potential operational problems [43], depending on the actual performance of the machine, which was not addressed in the current research. Miscalibration of trust will directly impair SA [7], as well as teaming [8], e.g., if an undertrusting team member keeps checking a robot that is actually performing well. Highly reliable robots may pose an additional challenge. Individuals prone to overtrust may lose vigilance for infrequent but important errors [55]. The high expectations PAS subscale [36] predicted trust in both types of scenario, i.e., it was positively associated with confidence and reliance on robot recommendations. Dispositional trust in automation may generalize to autonomous robots making various types of analysis, including psychological ones. System reliability is important for trust regardless of the type of analysis performed.

Turning from overall to more specialized forms of trust, the operator’s technical knowledge of the system is likely to inform physics-based trust. The mental model can be optimized through technical training and instruction that may correct any pre-existing faulty beliefs, such as excessively high or low expectations. A remaining issue is optimizing trust in robots whose behaviors change over time as a consequence of inscrutable machine learning algorithms [12]. Individual biases may delay dynamic trust recalibration as machine functioning changes, leading to poor team SA and team performance as mentioned above.

Optimizing psychological trust may be a more complex issue due to preexisting dispositional factors [42]. Some individuals may have trouble imagining how an artificial system can perform humanlike functions, a bias that may be difficult to counter through technical instruction. The multiple regression analysis here confirmed that negative attitudes toward robots may be uniquely associated with lower trust in robots making psychological judgments. Specifically, the role of the NARS negative emotions subscale in this article implies that some individuals may be biased because they are repelled by humanoid machines that simulate emotional functioning. Subscale items refer to interactions with robots such as how relaxed the person would feel talking with robots and their level of comfort with robot emotion. By contrast, the “social” subscale, which was less predictive of trust, refers to apprehensions about robots dominating society. In some people, the mental model may encode rejection of the notion of robots as entities that can function psychologically. Strong rejection of this type is liable to impede teaming with autonomous agents, an issue that may become more severe as AI becomes more sophisticated, negating the benefits of teamwork. Undertrust and disuse may occur in situations where an autonomous partner is actually well equipped to reduce the operator’s workload but the partner is disinclined to rely on a social robot. Additionally, hostility to a robot partner may lead to maladaptive teaming processes, such as denigrating robot capabilities to other human teammates and assigning unnecessary increases in workload across team members.

Training and design solutions to undertrust might focus on factors known to enhance acceptance of social agency in robots, including positive utilitarian and hedonic experiences of interacting with the robot, confidence, and positive social norms for working with robots [24]. For example, training exercises could be designed to highlight the value and ease of working with a robot. The instructor could emphasize organizational acceptance of robot collaboration and the benefits for other human teammates across the larger organization.

By contrast, psychological overtrust may also be an issue for some individuals. The anthropomorphizing tendency may limit justified skepticism about robot capabilities. If the machine is perceived as a kind of person, it may be natural to assume that it can detect emotions as a person does, especially if design factors promote sympathetic identification with the machine [56], [57]. People that overtrust the robot’s psychological capacities may overlook contextual factors that even humans find challenging when making psychological evaluations (e.g., [58]). Predicting aggressive behavior from an angry facial expression also requires us to identify the source of anger, how important the issue is to the person, the likelihood that anger will motivate action, and additional factors such as cultural norms for anger expression. Training for individuals who overtrust agent psychological judgments might focus on the difficulties of making predictive psychological inferences and agent fallibility in this respect. For example, exercises could be designed to highlight task activities that are assignable to the robot but only the human can perform competently.

## B. Implications for Design of Transparency

As previously discussed, transparency provides a general approach to optimizing trust through enhancing the operator’s understanding of various aspects of system functioning [4]. The current research identifies faulty beliefs encoded in mental models as a source of trust miscalibration, which may be remediated through transparency. Current work [4], [20] may be leveraged to address trust optimization for intelligent systems, subject to known issues, such as possible increased workload from transparency information [59]. For example, in terms of the SAT model [20], trust may be optimized by clarifying the robot’s purposes and processes for extracting basic information (Level 1), the principles it utilizes for high-level comprehension (Level 2), and its ability to project its future actions (Level 3).

A novel implication of the study is that transparency might be configurable according to contextual factors and operator disposition. Different forms of transparency may work better according to 1) whether a tool or teammate mental model is activated in a given HRT context and 2) whether the mental model encourages over- or undertrust. When the robot is perceived as an advanced tool, transparency can be guided primarily by existing models [4], but complexity and incomprehensibility remain challenging. Simplified information on robot functioning may suffice. A more radical and somewhat paradoxical proposal is to attribute humanlike “intuition” to the robot, even when making physics-based analyses. Human experts often make decisions based on unconscious, procedural knowledge, rather than explicit reasoning [60]. Other humans commonly trust those judgments provided that the expert is perceived as a credible source [61]. Perhaps humans can be trained to accept robot “intuition,” with transparency based on the robot justifying the credibility of its otherwise inscrutable algorithms. Transparency of this kind may work better for individuals disposed to attribute positive human qualities to robots.

In contexts where the robot is perceived as functioning like a human teammate, design of transparency may need to accommodate bias in the robot-as-teammate mental model. In terms of the SAT model [20], Level 2 may be the critical one for transparency [62], as it represents information about the rationale for the robot’s integration of lower level information to support a situation interpretation that guides action recommendations. In making psychological judgments about potential human threats, the robot functions like a human in interpreting cues such as facial expression to make attributions about emotion and intention. Transparency information that explains how a machine can validly make such attributions may be especially valuable for calibrating trust in those individuals prone to suspicion of robots. For example, the robot could signal which sensors it is using in analyzing emotion to draw attention to its technical capabilities. Conversely, overtrusting humans may benefit from transparency on the limitations of the robot’s analysis, including information on areas of uncertainty or missing data [63]. The robot may estimate its likely error rate, or ask the human to check for contextual factors that might influence a display of emotion.

Especially in contexts in which the teammate mental model dominates, humanlike feedback may play a key role [64]. Indeed, humanness may be essential for matching user perceptions with the capabilities of artificial intelligence [65]. Robot facial expressions can provide both task-related intentional information and teaming-related information on robot and human states in support of trust calibration [66]. Empathetic expressions may counter undertrust and expressions of confusion or doubt may limit overtrust. Forms of messaging that support a distrustful human teammate may also help robot-to-human communication. For example, a robot that needs to take over a responsibility from a distrustful human teammate might use a sympathetic vocal tone or facial expression, signaling that it had the benevolent motivation of reducing strain on the human. Different messaging might be necessary for the overtrustful human, e.g., the robot might signal lack of confidence in its recommendation, prompting the human to check.

## C. Study Limitations

Several limitations should be noted. First, evaluation of trust depended on subjective ratings of hypothetical scenarios and findings require confirmation from behavioral studies. Second, participants had no special expertise in security operations; it is unclear whether results would generalize to real security personnel. Similarly, the study does not capture trust dynamics operating during security operations conducted in real time.

Third, this article represents a first attempt to determine the value of discriminating different mental models and the individual difference factors associated with them. Thus, we have only limited evidence for construct validity of the scenario-based RoTA scale for trust in autonomy. Further work is necessary to determine its convergent and divergent validity. Such work might include measurement of standard personality traits and aspects of mental models that are not captured by the NARS and PAS. In line with existing justifications for SJTs [52], the scenario-based approach may provide greater validity for the specific security context than general assessments of trust or broad personality traits. However, this hypothesis requires confirmation, for example, in a study predicting trust in a more realistic simulation or field study. The assessment is also geared toward detecting bias rather than accuracy of evaluating the robot, as there is no benchmark for actual robot competence in the scenarios. Further work might explore contexts in which robot performance can be objectively set or rated by experts.

Fourth, the scenarios comprising the RoTA scale focus on trust in the robot’s judgments of threat, but involve limited teamwork. More complex scenarios would entail a greater teamwork focus. For example, the robot might take autonomous decisions about where and how to detect threats, taking into account and communicating its assessment of human capabilities (robot-of-human transparency [4]). Further work is needed to determine which mental models might predominate as the robot assumes greater autonomy, authority, and intelligent reactivity to human teammate functioning.

## V. CONCLUSION

People’s interactions with intelligent, autonomous systems may be influenced by the predominant mental model in the context of the interaction. The presented findings suggested that both the type of analysis performed by the robot and individual difference factors may influence the mental model that is activated. Biases in the mental model such as irrational expectations or rejection of robots with humanlike qualities may lead to suboptimal trust and impaired SA. Designing appropriate transparency that can be configured to contextual and user characteristics provides a strategy for trust management. Future research should address the use of transparency to overcome the challenges of machine intelligence including incomprehensibility and human discomfort with social agency in robots.
